# Nuclear radiation hazards

## 1. Introduction

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Nuclear radiation hazards

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Ionising radiation — alpha, beta, gamma, X-rays — strips electrons from atoms, breaking DNA and killing or mutating cells. Sources are natural (cosmic rays, radon, rocks) and man-made (reactors, weapons, medical use, waste). Hazard depends on dose, duration and penetration; protection rests on **time, distance and shielding**.

**Concept flow — from source to safety rule (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Natural background | Cosmic rays, radon gas from rock, K-40 in food — always present |
| 2 | Man-made sources | Medical X-rays (largest artificial dose), reactors, weapons testing, radioisotopes |
| 3 | Biological damage | Ionisation breaks DNA: cell death, mutations, cancer |
| 4 | Acute vs chronic exposure | High short dose → radiation sickness; low long dose → cancer risk |
| 5 | Penetration rules | Alpha stopped by paper; beta by aluminium; gamma needs thick lead/concrete |
| 6 | Protection triad | Minimise TIME, maximise DISTANCE, use SHIELDING |
| 7 | Waste problem | Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years — deep geological storage |

**Alpha, beta, gamma — the three radiations compared**

| Property | Alpha (α) | Beta (β) | Gamma (γ) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nature | Helium nucleus (2p + 2n) | Fast electron | High-energy electromagnetic wave |
| Penetration | Stopped by paper or skin | Stopped by a few mm of aluminium | Needs thick lead or concrete |
| Internal hazard | Most dangerous if INHALED/ingested | Moderate | Dangerous from outside — deep penetration |
| Ionising power | Highest | Moderate | Lowest per interaction |
| Example source | Radon, americium in smoke detectors | Sr-90, C-14 | Co-60, Cs-137 |

**Radiation effects classified by dose and timing**

| Exposure | Effect | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Acute, whole body, very high | Radiation sickness: nausea, hair loss, marrow failure, death | Reactor accidents (Chernobyl firefighters) |
| Chronic, low level | Raised cancer risk over years; mutations in gametes | Survivors near test sites; occupational exposure |
| Localised | Skin burns, local tissue death | Industrial source mishandling |
| In utero | Developmental damage | Medical exposure of pregnant women — avoided |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — choosing the shield.** A lab stores three sources: an alpha emitter (Am-241), a beta emitter (Sr-90) and a gamma emitter (Co-60). The alpha source needs only a sealed container — its danger is inhalation, not penetration. The beta source needs a few millimetres of aluminium. The gamma source needs a lead brick bunker and a distance rule, because gamma slices through ordinary shields. One property — penetration — decides the whole safety plan.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Ionising radiation damages DNA; hazard = type × dose × duration; protection = time, distance, shielding. Alpha in, gamma out — remember that pairing. **Self-check:** can you match each radiation to its stopping material?

mcqs.question: A common examiner point on "Nuclear radiation hazards" is that a statement is only valid when its condition of applicability is met. Is that TRUE or FALSE?
mcqs.explanation: Every NEB rule has a scope (e.g. a specific range, temperature, or sign convention); stating the condition earns full marks.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Radiation types: alpha (stopped by skin/paper), beta (penetrates skin), gamma (deep penetration, most dangerous) — the penetration ladder.
Trick 2: Effects: somatic (cancer, burns, leukaemia in the exposed person) vs genetic (mutations in offspring) — the two-class division.
Trick 3: Case studies: Chernobyl (1986), Fukushima (2011), Hiroshima/Nagasaki — quote one with its lesson.
Trick 4: Radioactive waste disposal: shielded storage, deep burial, vitrification — the three strategies; half-life governs storage time.
